claims.text: At high temperature, FeNiCrCoCu thin-coating wear resistance is governed by in situ formation of a stable, passivating oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer forms at microstructural grain boundaries.
The oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and wear.
The initial FeNiCrCoCu coating has a fine-grained microstructure.
Oxidation is minimal during the proposed room-temperature baseline tests.
Elevated temperature promotes selective oxidation of one or more FeNiCrCoCu constituents at grain boundaries.
Selective grain-boundary oxidation produces a continuous oxide film.
The continuous oxide film acts as both a lubricant and a barrier against wear.
The oxide film lowers wear by minimizing direct contact between the sliding surfaces.
At approximately 500 degrees Celsius or above in an oxidative environment, the coating will have a significantly lower wear rate than at room temperature.
At approximately 500 degrees Celsius or above, the coating will exhibit a more stable friction coefficient than at room temperature.
Lower high-temperature wear and more stable friction will coincide with a continuous oxide layer detectable by XPS or SEM-EDS.
Room-temperature FeNiCrCoCu coatings without a significant oxide film typically experience higher wear because of unprotected metal contact.
A temperature of approximately 500 degrees Celsius or greater is sufficient to drive appreciable oxidation under the proposed conditions.
Oxide-layer continuity may vary with compositional inhomogeneity or grain size.
